newsitem.title: USA: A survivor, Washington mayor faces new challenge.
newsitem.headline: A survivor, Washington mayor faces new challenge.

text.p: In life, he has survived prostate cancer and a shotgun wound to the chest. In politics, being shown on national television smoking crack cocaine was no impediment to his being twice returned to elected office.

Now Marion Barry faces a recall movement that seeks to remove him from office as mayor of Washington, D.C., the crime-ridden capital of the United States that is home to nearly 600,000 people, most of them black, like Barry himself.

The issue threatens to further divide the city along racial lines as the effort to disloge Barry has found enthusiastic support among whites and a chilly if not hostile response from many blacks, recall leaders say.
It is yet another test for one of the most controversial and remarkable figures in American politics as Barry also contemplates whether to seek a fifth term as mayor next year.

"After he went to prison he said he was rehabilitated, but he just told lies again," recall leader Sandra Seegars, a black former Barry supporter, told Reuters. "Marion Barry is selling out the city at wholesale prices."
Seegars charges Barry is a corrupt, two-faced politician whose cronies get rich on city contracts.

Barry press secretary Raymone Bain told Reuters the mayor would not respond to questions about the recall movement. "His position is that the people have the right to do what they want to do," Bain said. "He feels he is a good mayor who is very concerned about the people of the district and is working hard for them. That's all that he has to say about it."

The idea of recalling Barry originated with taxi driver Nathan Price, who also is black, and was latched onto by Seegars, who publishes a quarterly newsletter in Barry's home district in the southeast section of Washington.

"When I was a kid the schools were segregated but it wasn't that bad. There wasn't crime in school and we had police on the beat," Price, president of the D.C. Professional Taxi Cab Drivers Association, told Reuters.
But to many African Americans in the capital city, Barry is a tireless fighter for the downtrodden who was instrumental in wresting control of the city from Congress in 1974.

Political analysts doubt the recall movement will succeed. The group must collect 34,000 valid signatures by Oct. 28 to put the issue on December's ballot but it is seeking 60,000 because election officials normally reject many as invalid.
Seegars refused to say how many have been collected since April, offering only that the group is on target for 34,000 but not 60,000. Price said the response had been "apathetic."

Barry, 60, the son of Mississippi sharecroppers, came to prominence in the 1960s civil rights movement. He was elected mayor in 1978 and was re-elected in 1982 and 1986. In 1990, he was caught on video tape smoking crack cocaine in an FBA sting operation. After six months in federal prison he was elected to the city council in 1992 and as mayor again in 1994.

While a city councilman in 1977, Barry was hit in the chest by a shotgun pellet when a radical Moslem group seized city hall. About a year and a half ago, he underwent surgery for prostate cancer and says today he is doing fine.
